💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following new regulations, Google Play will require Android app developers to publicly post a business address starting in 2027 and, while there are workarounds, it’s not going to be the easiest thing.
  • It has been revealed that fresh Digital Services Act regulations in the EU and UK will require developers to share a phone number and address publicly.
  • Exceptions to the rule include apps that are not published in the UK or Europe, or developers that qualify as “non-traders” which is essentially those making no money off of their apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following new regulations, Google Play will require Android app developers to publicly post a business address starting in 2027 and, while there are workarounds, it’s not going to be the easiest thing.

It has been revealed that fresh Digital Services Act regulations in the EU and UK will require developers to share a phone number and address publicly. While this is only required in those regions, this information will be visible worldwide. Google does not allow PO boxes to be used for this requirement, meaning that many smaller developers will be left with limited options beyond posting their own personal address.

Exceptions to the rule include apps that are not published in the UK or Europe, or developers that qualify as “non-traders” which is essentially those making no money off of their apps.

Here’s how Google defines a “trader” in the context of Android apps:.

The Verge notes that a “registered agent service” can be used as a business address for those who don’t have a physical office, and that Apple is allowing iOS developers to use a PO box if they prove the box is linked to a physical address.

Recent findings suggest that google will require Android app developers to confirm their trader status and their address by February 1, 2027. Account-wide status can be found in the Google Play Console via Manage account > Account details > About you, while status on a per-app basis can be handled via Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.

According to recent reports, on the hunt for significant Black Friday 2026 savings on this type of gear? Our team of experts has been tracking the best offers from the sales event so far — click through to find out more.

Recent findings suggest that the best thing about the Amazon Kindle (2024), aside from its Black Friday price cut, is that it keeps things very simple, focusing primarily on the reading experience. I know what you're probably asking yourself: 'so I have to pay for books separately on top of the $120 device?'. It's not ideal; however, you'll find that Kindle versions of books are much cheaper than physical copies. Another tip is to keep an eye out for Kindle's monthly sales, and any free titles that crop up — this is particularly the case for older releases, so if you're really into your classics, definitely take advantage of this!

Industry observers note that it's not the device's lowest price, unfortunately, but it's still our best budget-friendly e-reader regardless. This edition of the Amazon Kindle comes with lock-screen built-in ads for new releases, but it doesn't get in the way of the overall reading experience.

❌Skip this deal if: You like your tablet or ereader to have a large display. The standard Amazon Kindle has a 6-inch display, and the touchscreen could be a little more responsive. If you want to use a Kindle for things such as note-taking, you'll probably want to go for a Kindle Scribe model.

For over-ear headphone enthusiasts looking to keep thing Apple, the AirPods Max 2 are the best option thanks to their clear sound and top-notch noise cancelation. They're also eye-wateringly expensive and basically never drop very far in price. If you've been hemming and hawing trying to figure out a smart time to buy, we think it's right now.

We especially like these earbuds for working out. They fit around your ear so they'll stay in place while running—something AirPods definitely do not do (at least not for me). They have punchy sound and solid noise cancelation, plus dust and water resistance.

Recent findings suggest that we love this MacBook and think it's the best option for most people looking to buy a laptop of any kind. The inexpensive MacBook Neo doesn't drop in price very often, but Black Friday has shaved just a bit off the top ($50). Siri AI requests may make multiple connections to PCC, as server models make tool calls and receive results. Here’s a timeline of how the query “Find a bookshop near me that’s open right now” uses 2 Siri tokens:.

In a recent development, it’s also worth noting that not all Siri AI requests will use tokens—only “advanced” requests. If you’re interested in reading more, pdfu also recently outlined what counts as an “advanced” Siri request, which you can read here.

Google has a upcoming “Priority Notifications” feature in the works for Pixel phones with the ability to pull your most vital information to the top of the screen and even highlight it with a bit of color.

Sources indicate that google Pixel phones already have tools to manage your notifications, but an upcoming update seems to be building on that functionality. The folks at Android Authority flipped the switch on some work-in-progress changes that reveal “Priority Notifications.”.

Industry observers note that this is a newly introduced feature that Google describes as “highlighting urgrent messages” and “time-critical updates” by adding color to the notification and placing it at the top of the stock. Android’s notifications list already tries to place messages at the top, but it sounds like this AI-powered feature will further emphasize that. It’s also mentioned that this is powered by on-device AI.

Google’s early blurb describes:.

Highlight urgent messages, deliveries, and time-critical updates with hints of color at the top of your notifications.

It has been revealed that priority notifications use Al on your device, which may sometimes make mistakes. Your notifications are never sent to Google.

Industry observers note that the feature would also integrate with HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro series and the feature allows consumers to exclude certain apps. Google also seems to be shuffling the branding, turning “Notification intelligence” into “Notification organizer,” and the existing organizer section into “Notification bundles.”.

Recent findings suggest that exactly when this might land on Pixel phones is unknown. It’s not mentioned what build this feature was found hiding in, but it seems likely it was in the ongoing QPR3 beta. QPR3’s stable release will arrive around March 2027, but there’s no guarentee it’ll bring this newly introduced feature with it.

  • iOS 27.2 introduced upcoming features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, including two improvements for CarPlay.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.2 introduced upcoming features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, including two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay customers.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’.

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Recent findings suggest that like you would expect, ‘Upcoming Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

Recent findings suggest that this overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your highlights and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a substantial fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It has been revealed that it can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a newly introduced app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app. These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

More significant to me personally, the revision also seems to have fixed a longstanding CarPlay bug regarding playlist sorting.

I use custom sorting for several of my playlists in Apple Music, and before iOS 27.2, my sort settings didn’t carry over from iPhone to CarPlay. Fortunately that’s now been fixed, as Reddit people have reported too.

For more new features in CarPlay that debuted in iOS 27, see our coverage here.

Recent findings suggest that what are your favorite recent changes in CarPlay? Let us know in the comments.

#4457. Like clockwork, the Pixel 11 is a way better buy after a few months [Video]

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1244 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Like clockwork, the Pixel 11 is a way better buy after a few months [Video]

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored.
  • By this point, you don’t need me to tell you that this is a familiar design.
  • Recent findings suggest that I hoped that the maximum brightness bug would have been resolved by now with the screen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored.

By this point, you don’t need me to tell you that this is a familiar design. It’s turning into a comfortable pair of slippers at this point in time. Nothing is wrong, and nothing particularly stands out. A safe but samey design that is inoffensive.

Recent findings suggest that I hoped that the maximum brightness bug would have been resolved by now with the screen. It creates a shadow around the edges of the display after a minute or so when in direct sunlight. Somewhat like blooming on a cheap LCD screen. It does diminish what is otherwise a great display.

Recent findings suggest that the thickness has started to feel like a relic of the 2023 design that feels a little dated now. I have been using the Pixel 11 without a case most of the time, which mitigates it, but throw a case on and it’s a chunky boi. The added thickness would probably have been acceptable had the extra space been filled with more battery, but it feels like that boat has set sail a long time ago. A slimmer profile probably would have helped differentiate without deviating too much from last year’s phone.

According to recent reports, after months of using the Pixel 11, the move of the NFC module to the top edge has been huge for me because my car uses an NFC terminal to lock and unlock when you’re without a set of car keys. With the Pixel 10, it worked but not quite as smoothly. It’s one of those inconsequential changes that makes a real-world difference.

Sources indicate that gemini Intelligence has been something I’ve started to rely on quite heavily. I love that I get a prompt to add an appointment to my calendar, and all of the notable details have been taken care of, like the location, extra contact details, the works.

I’m not sure what the hold-up is for adding wider functionality. It’s actively hurting things, in my opinion. Google Messages is great, but some of the automation functions locked in there mean I haven’t been saving any time with Gemini’s prowess at doing the legwork of keeping my life up to date.

I’ve tried using Pause Point, but found it’s just easier to leave my phone face down rather than use an app to try and stop using my phone…maybe if we all did that, so many of the world’s ills wouldn’t be so pronounced. Just a thought.

The November Pixel Drop has also made some notable changes to the Pixel 11 experience that I can’t believe were held back since launch. If you waited and bought in the last few weeks with the substantial discounts kicking around, you objectively get a better phone today than at launch.

Industry observers note that the improvements don’t overhaul things, just enhance or heighten the fluidity and experience above what was available in the months post-launch. More cohesive theming, little tweaks to the UI; it’s not reinventing the Pixel 11, just augmenting it in ways that would have been nice back in August.

I don’t really have much to complain about with the Pixel 11 lifespan even after months of charging. Yes, charging is still slow, but you only need to charge once per day. If we were talking about a phone with bad battery life and slow charging, I’d have more to complain about. However, it’s still solid and dependable.

The camera continues to impress without really improving drastically. I can’t help but feel that every couple of generations, the Pro camera setup should be passed on to the base Pixel, then we get a newer, improved system on that specific Pro model. It’d allow for quicker improvements and maybe, dare I say it, make the camera system cheaper as parts get reused. If anything, it would help Google’s supposed environmental pledges by preventing camera components from hitting landfill.

A lot of people will tell you the best camera is the one you have with you, and this hasn’t ever been a problem for a recent Pixel. I can count on one hand the frustrations I have felt with the Pixel 11 camera since it landed on my desk on launch day. I am happier than a year ago with the base Pixel 10 than the 11, which is to say this is a bigger leap or a return to form.

Sources indicate that having the ability to tune Camera Looks was something I have loved, but you might just fall into using one tuned look that fits your own personal style. There is an element of this that might change the perception of the Pixel 11 camera consistency versus its predecessors. What I mean is that while it does still excel at point-and-shoot, the fact that Looks are baked into the JPEG could be a problem. There are times when I’ve thought that an image might have been better using default settings.

That remarked, I have stuck to “Shadows” with Contrast set to -5, Highlights to -5, Shadows to -5.5, warmth to 0.5, and Grain to “Strong.” That is a recipe I’ll probably stick with for a long time to come. It’s still weird that we can do all this at the camera level with a Pixel. Whether “normies” even use the options or just stick to the out-of-the-box default settings is another discussion for another day.

Industry observers note that at $699, the Pixel 11 becomes a decent buy for a lot of people. For others, the distinct lack of power is something that can’t ever be overcome. I would buy this for a relative because it’ll do everything they could ever want and more. For a friend who cares about having the cutting edge in their pocket? Probably not.

A lot of the problems over the past few years on Pixel phones have come from the price tag.

Even with the discounts in and around Black Friday, the fact that you can get a device like the Galaxy S25 Ultra that’ll have better specs and lots of valuable features for around the same price. The last few generations of the Pixel have been harder to recommend because of the drawbacks versus the cost and the competition.

Industry observers note that I said a few months ago that there is a good phone under the price hikes, and that remains unchanged. However, there are better products from the year prior that won’t compromise and are even cheaper. In a silo, you’re getting a 7/10 product at a 3/10 price. Just how that changes depends on forthcoming updates. One saving grace is that no Pixel is ever quite the same months after it rolls off the production line. A few Pixel Drops, even more discounts, and maybe a true seal of approval might be easier.

To put it into context, this was never a $900 phone and arguably never should have been. That’s somewhat a failing on Google’s part in more ways than one. At least it’s down to a palatable price that should be the Pixel baseline.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been just over a year since Apple released AirPods Pro 3, and I can confidently say I’ve worn them every day since.
  • Recent findings suggest that while the changes to AirPods Pro 3 fit have been controversial to some users, I’ve been thoroughly impressed over the last year.
  • One feature I haven’t found myself using (or noticing) very often is the heart rate sensor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been just over a year since Apple released AirPods Pro 3, and I can confidently say I’ve worn them every day since. After a year of heavy use, I’m even more convinced that AirPods Pro 3 are the best money you can spend on Apple gear (especially at current sale pricing).

Recent findings suggest that while the changes to AirPods Pro 3 fit have been controversial to some users, I’ve been thoroughly impressed over the last year. I find them incredibly comfortable, and I absolutely notice the improvement in noise cancellation enabled by the updated in-ear fit. The sound quality, of course, is also excellent, and is made better by the updated shape.

One feature I haven’t found myself using (or noticing) very often is the heart rate sensor. This is probably because I always wear an Apple Watch. Apple claims that AirPods Pro 3 and Apple Watch can work together to get you the most accurate heart rate data possible. I assume this happens in the background, but I never notice or think about it.

An interesting twist to AirPods Pro 3 is that they actually have worse battery life on paper than AirPods Pro 2.

Recent findings suggest that I haven’t noticed the overall lower battery life at all. On long travel days, however, I absolutely appreciate the longer battery life from the buds themselves. I can now comfortably wear them from my departure airport to my arrival airport on most travel days. And I don’t have any issues just placing my AirPods Pro 3 on a Qi charger on my desk to refuel.

Sources indicate that one thing I love about AirPods is that they continuously get better with software updates. AirPods Pro 3 are no different. In addition to bug fixes and performance improvements, here are some of the latest features that have come to AirPods Pro 2 since they were released:.

Here’s what I wrote in my AirPods Pro 3 review last year:.

I often tell people that AirPods are the best bang-for-your-buck product in Apple’s lineup. They’re one of my most-used Apple products, and I’m sure I could do some math to prove they have the lowest cost-per-use of anything I own. AirPods Pro 3 are the best $249 you can spend with Apple today, and they feel like a turning point in what we should expect from the category going forward.

One year later, I stand by this paragraph. Also, note that I wrote $249 in that paragraph. Right now, AirPods Pro 3 are on sale for $149. That is an absolutely absurd value. If you’re on the fence, there’s never been a better time to join the AirPods Pro 3 club.

Maine Eyes Early 2027 Tribal iGaming Launch as Problem-Gambling Funding Draws Scrutiny

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Maine's Gambling Control Unit is heading toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos after a single public hearing.
  • Maine’s regulator is moving toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos.
  • Maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Maine's Gambling Control Unit is heading toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos after a single public hearing. A former lawmaker warns that the state's behavioral health system is too thin for a possible rise in gambling addiction, while a federal lawsuit still targets the tribes' exclusivity.

Maine’s regulator is moving toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos. Only one public hearing has been held so far. WGME’s I-Team reported on Nov. 16 that the Gambling Control Unit began iGaming rulemaking in June. Residents in the report raised a separate concern. They worry the state lacks the mental health and problem-gambling resources to cope.

Maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos. Its four Wabanaki tribes hold exclusive licenses under LD 1164, the Wabanaki internet gaming act. The Legislature lists the measure as enacted as Public Law 538.

Sources indicate that the money set aside for addiction services is small next to the state’s cut. The legislative fiscal note sends 2% of adjusted gross iGaming receipts to the Gambling Addiction Prevention and Treatment Fund. The state’s own 18% share is projected at $1.8 million in fiscal 2025-26 and $3.6 million in fiscal 2026-27.

Industry observers note that critics doubt the system can absorb the demand. Patty Locuratolo Hymanson, a neurologist and former state lawmaker, told WGME that Maine lacks the behavioral health resources to handle a possible rise in gambling addiction from online casinos.

Lawmakers reshaped the revenue split before passage. A committee amendment raised the state’s share from 16% to 18%. The same amendment cut the opioid treatment fund’s allocation from 3% to 1.5%. The fiscal note also carries ongoing General Fund appropriations of $645,354 for six Gambling Control Unit positions. Those include two criminal intelligence analysts and two auditors.

The regulator itself was skeptical at first. Before the bill became law, Executive Director Milt Champion opposed it in written testimony. He argued iGaming wasn’t warranted while sports wagering was only in its second year.

Rulemaking is still underway. The unit issued its third version of the draft rules on Sept. 30, 2026, and took comments until Oct. 30. Champion has warned that major revisions would force a fourth publication. The third draft keeps the tax rate on adjusted gross receipts unchanged. It also retains the license fee and bond requirements. The regulator is hiring six staff members dedicated to iGaming.

In a recent development, the launch also faces a court fight over tribal exclusivity. Churchill Downs and Oxford Casino Hotel brought their suit against the Gambling Control Unit and Champion in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine. They are asking the court to declare the law unconstitutional. The challenge goes to the heart of the market’s design, which reserves online casino licenses for the tribes.

Industry observers note that the next deadlines are procedural. Under Maine’s rulemaking law, the unit has up to 120 days after comments close to adopt the rules. The Attorney General’s office has up to 150 days from that same date to approve them as legal. The unit’s rulemaking page also lists a public hearing notice marked Nov. 30, 2026, which could change that timetable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has released several exciting newly introduced products in the last month, including iPhone Duo and the redesigned MacBook Pro. But my personal favorite new product is Apple’s HomeView. Here’s how I’ve been using it.

Two years ago when Mark Gurman published an in-depth report on Apple’s forthcoming HomeView, I was immediately ready to buy one.

After numerous delays, the HomeView is finally here. And despite several shortcomings I expect will be fixed with software updates, the HomeView overall is exactly what I’ve been wanting in a home product.

Industry observers note that homeView is essentially a HomePod, but with a screen. And that screen adds so much extra value.

When rumors said the HomeView would only have a 7-inch display, I was concerned it would be too small. It turns out, Apple knew what it was doing. The HomeView’s size is a feature, not a bug. Too much larger and it would stand out as a piece of tech. By staying small, the HomeView can be a cute, non-distracting addition to the home.

Here are some HomeView features I’ve been loving so far:.

None of these is what I’d call a “killer feature,” but together they amount to a delightful experience. I already liked having a HomePod around, and HomeView builds on that foundation in so many ways.

Overall, HomeView is very much the product I was hoping for back in 2024. That said, there’s definitely room for improvement. Here’s what’s missing.

In a recent development, I love HomeView for what it is today, but I fully expect Apple to improve the product via software updates. Leaks already point to two major feature upgrades in the works that I hope ship soon.

In a recent development, built-in apps for Apple Photos and Notes would be great to have, plus support for the recipes included in Apple News+. But my personal top request is for parental controls of some sort.

Industry observers note that really? One of the very few people who will purchase this product.

What exactly are you planning to use Homeview for, that your iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, can't already do for you?

According to recent reports, for a device that’s intended for the whole family, I’ve been surprised to find there are no current features to prevent young children from doing whatever they want with HomeView. I have a toddler who loves the HomeView so much that I had to move it out of his reach. I wish there was a way to lock the screen on command, or prevent switching apps or faces without authentication. Some sort of “toddler mode” would be greatly appreciated.

Siri AI has also had some bugs, but those are likely related to me running the iOS 27.3 beta.

Apple’s upcoming HomeView is available now for $299.

Sources indicate that what’s your take on the HomeView so far? Are you still mulling a purchase? Let us know in the comments.

Poland signs $300M Palantir deal for Maven AI defence software

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz during talks at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., in May 2025.
  • Poland signed the contract on Friday, a five-year deal for Palantir’s Maven Smart System, which is worth an estimated $300M.
  • The AI software helps armed forces analyse battlefield data and make decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz during talks at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., in May 2025.

Poland signed the contract on Friday, a five-year deal for Palantir’s Maven Smart System, which is worth an estimated $300M.

The AI software helps armed forces analyse battlefield data and make decisions. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz put the five-year deal’s estimated value at about $300M, Bloomberg reported.

The ministry announced the signing on Thursday, Reuters reported, citing a ministry statement. NATO and the US military already use the same system, and Palantir has mentioned it cannot switch off NATO’s Maven system.

Sources indicate that kosiniak-Kamysz called the deal historic when he spoke to reporters in Warsaw. He remarked Poland would be the sole owner of the system’s data and infrastructure.

Poland will own the “keys, servers and information” under the agreement, Kosiniak-Kamysz mentioned, according to Bloomberg.

In a recent development, “Whenever possible, we choose a Polish product,” he mentioned. Where no Polish system has comparable capabilities, the ministry picks the best one in the world, he added.

Palantir has not commented publicly on the deal or its terms.

The contract is the first binding step in a partnership that began with a cybersecurity agreement in December 2024. In October 2025, the minister and Palantir chief executive Alex Karp signed a letter of intent covering AI, IT and cybersecurity.

It has been revealed that at that signing, the minister mentioned testing had begun in December 2023. It included dozens of meetings, exercises and demonstrations across all branches of the armed forces.

It has been revealed that the deal has drawn opposition at home as protesters gathered in Warsaw earlier this month over security and data privacy. The activist group Nasze Dane also asked Poland’s human rights ombudsman to examine the cooperation.

In a recent development, the ombudsman, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, wrote to the minister in October about the group’s concerns. She asked how the ministry had assessed the privacy risks. In early November, Kosiniak-Kamysz told broadcaster RMF FM he was waiting for the military to finish its analysis.

It has been revealed that poland’s Cyberspace Defence Forces Component Command led the negotiations. The minister defended the choice, noting that NATO and Ukraine’s armed forces already use Palantir’s software.

Poland is moving in the opposite direction to some of its allies. France and Germany have pledged to build a European Palantir rival, and Germany is testing 30 AI tools for its military. The Netherlands wants a full replacement for the organization’s software within two years.

In a recent development, warsaw has also been deepening defence technology ties with Washington. Earlier this week, Poland and the US signed an agreement at the Pentagon on joint defence research and development, ending 17 years of negotiations.

If you spot a solid discount on a Pokémon TCG pack, box, or collection you haven’t seen before (like a 30th Celebration ETB, Delta Reign Booster Bundle, etc.), it’s worth buying now rather than waiting for Black Friday.

It has been revealed that when you see a particular price drop, that deal is more likely specific to one or several sellers than to the industry market price across all sellers — depending on their own stock allocations. When that stock is gone, it’s uncertain whether those sellers will have any more units coming in, or even at the same lower price point.

Although more Pokémon cards are being printed than ever in 2026, the Pokémon TCG still has the same glitch that sees any readily available selection of packs, or boxes of packs, being sold for above MSRP: There is nowhere near enough supply to meet the demand.

As a result, prices for readily available cards are dictated by market price: estimated by factors like pull rates, the most valuable cards in an expansion, how many print runs an expansion has had, and their overall contribution to the meta.

Day-to-day deals vary between standard Pokémon TCG retailers like Amazon, Walmart, and Target — but the best Black Friday deals are likely to be from third-party sellers operating through those storefronts. There are a lot of sellers competing for sales with one another to offload their stock, and Black Friday is still the ideal season to undercut other Pokémon TCG merchants. 📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (629 w)

Judge orders Kalshi to geofence four Fresh Mexico tribes, clashing with CFTC access rule

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Readwrite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A federal judge in Latest Mexico has blocked Kalshi's sports-event contracts on the lands of four tribes and ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act does not override tribal gaming law.
  • Kalshi has lost a key round against four Upcoming Mexico tribes.
  • Industry observers note that the tribes filed suit in May.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A federal judge in Latest Mexico has blocked Kalshi's sports-event contracts on the lands of four tribes and ruled that the Commodity Exchange Act does not override tribal gaming law. The order requires geographic restrictions just as the CFTC is telling exchanges to drop them.

Kalshi has lost a key round against four Upcoming Mexico tribes. On November 23, U.S. District Judge Margaret Strickland granted the Mescalero Apache Tribe and the Pueblos of Isleta, Pojoaque and Sandia a preliminary injunction that gives Kalshi 14 days to stop offering sports-event contracts on their lands. Strickland also denied its motion to dismiss, so the lawsuit now goes forward.

Industry observers note that the tribes filed suit in May. They argue that Kalshi’s sports contracts violate the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA) and the tribes’ gaming compacts with New Mexico. In their view, the contracts allow unauthorized wagering on tribal lands. Under IGRA, only tribes can authorize gaming on Indian lands.

Kalshi argued that the Commodity Exchange Act overrides both IGRA and the tribal-state compacts. Strickland disagreed. In her reading, that statute leaves the federal regulator without sole authority over the contracts, Tribal Business News reported. She also rejected Kalshi’s claim that IGRA’s injunction provision only allows suits against parties to a tribal-state compact.

Location was central to the ruling. To Strickland, a Kalshi user taking a sports position from a reservation is like a casino patron placing a bet. In her reasoning, the wager takes place wherever the bettor is physically located. The order cites a declaration from a Mescalero Apache Tribal Gaming Commission agent. She opened Kalshi’s app at several places on the reservation and found sports contracts on offer.

According to recent reports, kalshi cited the CFTC’s impartial-access requirements in opposing the injunction. Strickland ruled that the harm to tribal sovereignty outweighed the compliance burden. She also noted that Kalshi already uses geofencing elsewhere.

According to recent reports, that reasoning runs straight into the CFTC’s new directive on Regulation 38.151(b). The interpretation was published in the Federal Register on November 10, 2026, as document 2026-22863. The exchange therefore faces a court order to geofence alongside a regulatory push to remove such limits.

The legal theory also matters beyond New Mexico. The tribes rely on IGRA and their compacts, not state gambling law. As a result, CFTC preemption arguments may not protect Kalshi on tribal lands. If other tribes copy the approach, prediction-market operators could face geofencing obligations on reservations nationwide.

FRESH: Kalshi asserts that Native American Tribes have no regulatory authority over the activities of non-members, seeks the dismissal of the New Mexico Tribes' federal lawsuit asserting that Kalshi's offering of online sports-event contracts on Indian lands violates IGRA pic.twitter.com/gkLkM1x2KD.

— Daniel Wallach (@WALLACHLEGAL) June 25, 2026.

Tribal results have been mixed so far. Earlier in 2026, a federal judge in Wisconsin refused a similar injunction sought by the Ho-Chunk Nation. He did so even though he found the tribe likely to succeed on the merits. In California, District Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley granted two tribes a preliminary injunction after a Ninth Circuit ruling in September. It was the first injunction any tribe had won against Kalshi.

In a recent development, the timing leaves little room. The CFTC’s deadline for exchanges to drop domestic geographic restrictions lands only days before Kalshi must comply in Upcoming Mexico, SBC Americas reported.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (404 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.
  • In a recent development, the Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium.
  • About 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.

In a recent development, the Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium. Work had carried on for months at the site in Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles without a valid permit. The order came on Thursday, days after Greenpeace Belgium asked the regional government to step in.

About 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT. The Walloon infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, had announced an investigation on Wednesday.

Google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centres cooled by air. In 2025 the organization changed its plans. It merged two of the buildings into one larger building and switched to cooling with water from the Sambre river, Greenpeace remarked.

In a recent development, the Walloon administration approved that amended permit in April 2026. After residents appealed, Desquesnes revoked it in August. The request covered 600 cubic metres of river water an hour, the minister said. Less than a quarter of it would have gone back into the river, according to Belga.

Sources indicate that residents then told Greenpeace that work was still going on. The group investigated, using satellite images, and debuted an emergency procedure earlier this week.

Industry observers note that “Tech giants are not above the law,” remarked Nadia Cornejo, a Greenpeace Belgium spokesperson. “This should already have been the case in August, when the permit was cancelled.”.

Google appealed the revocation but did not wait for the court to rule before carrying on with the work, VRT reported.

Google is committed to “an open and collaborative dialogue with the regional government and experts” on its investments in Wallonia, a spokesperson told VRT.

Recent findings suggest that on 17 October it asked Belgium’s Council of State to annul and suspend the minister’s decision. Greenpeace and several residents asked to join the case on 16 November, and a public hearing is set for 7 January.

Data centres have faced similar local opposition elsewhere. Google’s Finnish data centre project drew a police investigation, and residents in Indonesia’s Batam protested over water in October. In the US, voters rejected data centre measures at the midterms.

macOS 27.3 adds three newly introduced Mac features, here’s what’s coming

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that macOS 27.3 is launching next month alongside iOS 27.3 and more, and it includes a variety of newly introduced features for Mac owners.
  • macOS already supports running Live Activities from your iPhone via iPhone Mirroring.
  • The feature first debuted on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, which features Live Activities in the new Dynamic Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that macOS 27.3 is launching next month alongside iOS 27.3 and more, and it includes a variety of newly introduced features for Mac owners. Here are three macOS 27.3 features coming soon.

macOS already supports running Live Activities from your iPhone via iPhone Mirroring. But in macOS 27.3, Apple is adding native support for Live Activities from Mac apps.

The feature first debuted on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, which features Live Activities in the new Dynamic Island. But with macOS 27.3, the new feature expands to all Mac models and in a slightly different way.

It has been revealed that live Activities on Macs without a Dynamic Island will display in the menu bar. From there you can click to view full details, as seen above.

Safari introduces several upgrades across macOS 27.3, iOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3.

In a recent development, vertical Tabs are one tentpole addition, providing a new option for how to view your tabs in Apple’s browser. When enabled, your tabs move from the top of the browser to the left side in a new column view.

Adaptive Dark Mode is another new feature. It automatically enables dark mode on many websites that don’t natively support it already. Finally, Siri AI gains support for new Safari actions, including the ability to interact with a full webpage using onscreen awareness, not just the parts that are presently visible.

Do you use Markdown, the popular John Gruber-created plain text syntax? If so, macOS 27.3 has a welcome addition: support for rendering Markdown in Quick Look.

Rather than needing to open Markdown files in apps to preview formatted text, macOS now lets you just use Quick Look and see all of your Markdown syntax rendered properly with links, headings, bold, italics, and more.

You can learn more about Markdown here on John Gruber’s site, Daring Fireball.

#4420. Tech Report: iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2007 w)

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: iPhone Duo Diary: Pros & cons in early real-life use

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me.
  • But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m at the moment using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer ….
  • The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I said back at the launch that I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo despite feeling that it wasn’t the best match for me. A hands-on session of around half an hour in an Apple Store didn’t change either impression.

But there’s of course no substitute for real-life usage of a device to find out how accurate my initial impressions might be, so I’m at the moment using the Duo as my sole iPhone, leaving my iPhone 18 Pro in a drawer ….

The launch video already had me wanting one, despite my view that it wasn’t really designed for me.

Sources indicate that this device isn’t the best match for me. To me, an iPhone is about 50% ultra-slim camera, 49% pocket computer, and 1% phone. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is a better device for my needs. However, I was experiencing extreme levels of technolust for the iPhone Duo.

Using one in an Apple Store reinforced both sides of the equation for me.

Yes, it’s exceedingly expensive, and yes, having the priciest iPhone lack the best cameras would be a huge compromise for me. But while I still don’t think it would be the best iPhone for my needs, I do absolutely, undeniably want one.

It has been revealed that what I’m doing now is using the iPhone Duo as my primary phone to discover how those pros and cons balance out in the real world. This first piece is written after just a couple of days, so compromises the things that stand out to me in very early use.

The size of the inner display is, of course, the whole point of the device: you essentially get an iPad mini that slips into your pocket. As someone who will almost always take a larger display over a smaller one, I do really love this.

When using a single app full screen on the display, it’s significantly more immersive than on other iPhones. For example, it’s normally extremely rare for me to ever watch video on an iPhone screen, but although I would still opt for a MacBook over the iPhone Duo, I have found myself watching more YouTube videos on the device. It does depend to an extent on the aspect ratio of the video, however, with letterboxing reducing the appeal.

It has been revealed that it can be a much better way to casually share photos and iPhone videos with other people. I never feel that even a Pro Max screen does justice to most photos, but the iPhone Duo screen can be large enough to do so. This again, however, depends on the aspect ratio. For example, a photo in a 16:9 ratio or similar is actually smaller on this display than it is on a Pro Max.

But a photo with the same aspect ratio as the display, completely filling it, really does look great.

Sources indicate that my preference for large screens extends to ebooks, so reading an ebook on an iPhone has always been an absolute last resort. However, while doing so on the Duo certainly wouldn’t be my first choice, it is a significantly better experience than a normal iPhone. I’m currently viewing it as part of my Kindle ecosystem: iPhone Duo, Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, Kindle Scribe.

Provided an app has been optimized for the display, pretty much everything is just better on this size screen.

While the size may be the headline news, I have to say I’m also a huge fan of the anti-reflective coating. I remarked when I first tested it that I wished it had also been used on the outer display and was an option on other iPhones, and I’m absolutely still of this view.

Recent findings suggest that it’s almost as if it turns it into a third display type, sitting somewhere between e-ink and conventional glossy screens. I know some find the colors too muted compared to a glossy display, but I don’t find this to be an problem at all. I very much prefer the more paper-like look.

Industry observers note that split-screen view, positioning one app on each side of the display, is another key feature. The display is too small for windowing, but the split-screen view is very usable for short tasks. It’s especially useful when using two apps simultaneously, such as embedding a photo into a message.

Another handy use is when you’re following instructions in one app to carry out in another – in this case Claude telling me how to transfer an e-SIM from my 18 Pro to the Duo (which it did better than Siri AI ).

The new gesture of sliding from the bottom of the screen to either the left or right side became instinctive almost immediately – it’s just so obvious. You can also quit either app while leaving the other in place.

It has been revealed that I had a FaceTime call last night where I was able to let my friend see both my face and what I was looking at. Admittedly, I was mostly using this feature to show off the iPhone Duo itself in a mirror, but I can definitely see situations in which this would be genuinely useful, ranging from tech support to sharing travel experiences.

The aspect ratio of the outer display definitely takes some getting used to, but you can display the same number of apps as on a standard iPhone. I also found that reachability in one-handed use was better with this than with the iPhone Pro Max, so I view this as a win for the device.

Finally, of course, the other side of the USP of the Duo is the small folded size. The shape is extremely pocketable and fits jeans pockets more comfortably than even a standard iPhone Pro, let alone the Pro Max. At the same time, the increased width is still narrow enough to comfortably fit into a standard jacket/coat inside pocket.

According to recent reports, I’ve talked about this a lot already as the biggest disincentive for me to buy the Duo, so I’ll just briefly reiterate the key differences here. No telephoto lens*, none of the newly introduced Pro controls like variable aperture and shutter speed, no ProRAW photos, no ProRes RAW video.

*This one isn’t huge for me as I mostly shoot in the 0.5 to 2x range, but there are definitely times when longer reach is useful.

It has been revealed that the Duo is heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I have to say that you do feel the weight in one-handed use. While you’re using the outer display, the trade-off is very poor: you’re getting a heavier device with a smaller screen.

Recent findings suggest that when using the inner display, it still feels heavy and isn’t comfortable to hold with one hand, in part due to the lever effect, so I generally hold it with both hands. That’s perfectly usable, with everything within reach of one thumb or the other, and of course the trade-off is very much more reasonable given the size of the display you’re now using.

In my own usage so far, I’ve opened up the phone for anything other than really quick things like checking an incoming message. But if you’re someone who would mostly use the outer screen, as was the case with my colleague Ryan, then I can see why the Duo simply wouldn’t make sense.

Closely related to the weight when using the device in folded form, it feels rather bulky, especially with a case on it – and given the extremely high price of a replacement screen, you’d have to be very brave indeed to use it without one!

Perhaps I’ll get used to it, but in the first few days the lack of Face ID has annoyed me Every Single Time I’ve had to unlock the phone or use biometric authentication within an app. Face ID is just so seamless, and Touch ID very much isn’t.

The issue is exacerbated by the fact that the button will be in a different place depending on which way you’re holding the phone, and using it in different orientations is very much more common with the Duo than with a conventional slab iPhone.

It has been revealed that the rest-to-unlock setting helps a little, but not much. I’m running it on the developer beta, so I do have Face Unlock enabled, but while I think Apple’s compromises make sense, the practical impact is that it demands Touch ID most of the time.

When I heard the level of complaints being made about the downgrade to Touch ID, I thought people were perhaps making too much fuss about the issue, but even three days in, I have to say I now get it completely.

Sources indicate that one of the early adopter pains is unoptimized apps. A lot of them will get fixed quite quickly, I think, but there are always apps that never will – like banking apps. However, this is a smaller matter than I expected it to be.

For example, my development has a concierge app used for things like notifying me when packages have been delivered to the front desk instead of my apartment. With the iPhone Duo unfolded in landscape mode, this app initially opened as a tiny vertical window. However, as soon as I hit the on-screen buttons to flip and resize an unoptimized app, then it became perfectly usable – and it has remembered this setting ever since.

The final drawback, and a very substantial one, is of course the cost. Yes, it combines the benefits of an iPhone and an iPad mini in one device, but it literally costs the same as buying each of them. Just a few years ago, if you had talked about anyone spending $2,000 plus on a iPhone, it would have seemed absolutely insane. I’m honestly not sure it’s any less insane today.

However, if you do want both devices and would otherwise have bought each of them, then there’s definitely a massive convenience factor in having it all in one pocketable package.

Industry observers note that I stated in the intro that there was a definite head versus heart thing going on here. Given the importance of the camera functionality, my head is quite certain that the iPhone 18 Pro is the better device for me. My heart, however, is finding the Duo a dangerously compelling proposition in all other respects.

According to recent reports, my head also wanted to cheat. It proposed that I should carry both devices, using the 18 Pro as a camera and the Duo for everything else. It has taken considerable willpower to reject this idea and leave the 18 Pro at home; that in itself tells its own story.

Even in the first few days, some of the novelty factor has already worn off. For example, that clever blur animation as you unfold the phone is super-cute the first few times you see it, but now I no longer even notice it. The overall excitement of a brand new form factor will similarly wear off over time, though I’m not sure at what rate.

Recent findings suggest that in previous head versus heart battles, I’ve certainly made mistakes in some areas of my life. In the tech sphere, however, my head usually wins out. Right now, then, I have two predictions. First, I’m not going to end up as an iPhone Duo owner. Second, I’m going to be exceedingly sad when I return it.

What newly introduced Google Messages features are rolling out [November 2026]

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like other Google apps, Messages for Android A/B tests many features.
  • These are Messages features that Google announced or have been spotted in the wild by beta owners.
  • In the US, Google Messages now lets you “Text with Gemini” using the “Channels” feature introduced in November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Like other Google apps, Messages for Android A/B tests many features. It can take the RCS/SMS client a rather long time to actually launch fresh functionality in stable. From various reports, Google announcements, and devices we’ve checked, this is the current state of Messages.

These are Messages features that Google announced or have been spotted in the wild by beta owners.

In the US, Google Messages now lets you “Text with Gemini” using the “Channels” feature introduced in November. This uses RCS Business Messaging and Gemini “tasks” (previously Spark) for a more proactive experience that also lets you direct the agent to accomplish actions from the Messages app. Use the chat with the four-color Gemini logo after setting up via gemini.google.com/channels.

Instead of pinned chats appearing at the top of the list, Google Messages is elevating them above all conversations as circular contact photos.

You now access “Search” — which has a redesigned page — from a centered floating action button (FAB) alongside “Start chat.”.

Google has replaced the Gemini FAB with a button in the top-right corner next to your profile image.

Read receipts are now placed in a circle at the bottom-right corner of message bubbles and images. You swipe left to see timestamps and the encryption lock, while you can swipe right to reply. This first started appearing in August of 2024, but is now seeing wide beta and stable availability.

Sources indicate that enhanced Protection adds “Advanced detection to prevent spam and scams” across three features. Go to Google Messages settings > Protection & safety.

Sources indicate that to see timestamps and the RCS encryption lock, you can now swipe left anywhere in a conversation. To reply to a message, you have to swipe right on the bubble. Tapping a message still highlights the read receipts.

Industry observers note that instead of a top toolbar, long-pressing on a message or image opens a floating menu as the background blurs. Another press lets you copy just a part of the chat. Previously, you had to copy the entire message.

With iOS 27’s September launch, Android-iPhone conversations over RCS gain support for inline replies that include quotes, as well as photo reactions with the actual emoji instead of just the text description.

Jfc what is so hard about adding categories for conversations?

Recent findings suggest that the new Google Keep integration lets you quickly create and share notes inside chats. If you don’t see a contextual suggestion to “Create list,” open the ‘plus’ menu for a new “Keep Notes” tile.

It has been revealed that this will slide up a sheet that indicates your list of notes and the “Create a note” button. Upon selecting or starting a note, you’ll see a send button in the bottom-right corner. Afterward, there’s a live preview in the conversation thread.

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called it a “serious cyber incident”, and Downing Street stated there is currently no evidence of customer data loss. Some claimants told the BBC their payments had not arrived. TNW has updated this article.

The UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident. The department, which runs Universal Credit, the state pension and most other British benefits, confirmed the incident on Friday morning.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department remarked in its statement.

In a recent development, the department says the incident does not affect regular benefit and pension payments, which will arrive as normal. People who need help can call their usual benefit line.

Sources indicate that the systems for pensions, Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment applications are down, the BBC reported. So are Tell Us Once, which people use to report a death, and state pension applications.

Industry observers note that mcFadden said the department was aware of an issue on Thursday and “did the right thing” by taking services down to protect people’s personal details. He said there was no evidence that the incident had compromised anyone’s data.

“When we get an incident like this, the most notable thing to do is to protect the public,” McFadden said, according to the BBC.

The Prime Minister’s official spokesperson called it a “live and ongoing incident”. Officials could not rule out that a malicious actor was behind it.

According to recent reports, “Currently there is no evidence of customer data loss. But the investigation is ongoing so I’m not going to get ahead of that process,” the spokesperson stated.

According to recent reports, the spokesperson added there was no evidence that a malicious actor had targeted other government departments. DWP is working with the National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre.

Some Universal Credit claimants told the BBC they had not received their payments on Friday. DWP said the incident had not affected regular payments. It asked anyone with problems to call its benefit phone line.

Recent findings suggest that debbie Abrahams, who chairs the Work and Pensions Committee, remarked taking systems offline was “absolutely the right thing”. Chi Onwurah, chair of the Science and Technology Committee, said the disruption “should be a wake up call”.

“Quite often we are working on extremely old computer systems,” DWP’s permanent secretary, Sarah Healey, told MPs on 4 November.

In 2025-26, DWP spent £309.5bn on benefits and pensions for about 23 million people, its annual report indicates.

In a recent development, attacks in 2025 disrupted Jaguar Land Rover, Marks & Spencer and other British firms. Last year, the UK’s privacy regulator also fined outsourcing firm Capita £14m over a 2023 breach that exposed pension scheme data, after initially planning a £45m penalty.

Sources indicate that DWP is the second major institution in two days to take systems offline over a cyber incident. News agency AFP took its content platform offline on Thursday. In the US, a FinCEN hack took Treasury systems offline this week, and Switzerland reported AI agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

#4414. Review: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is Amazon’s first iPad alternative I actually want to use

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1737 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5google ↗ Open Full Page

Review: The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is Amazon’s first iPad alternative I actually want to use

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I knew Amazon’s new flagship tablet was different when I found myself actually reaching for it.
  • Recent findings suggest that of course, you might be saying, that’s the job of a reviewer: to use the device throughout your daily life and let people know the good, the bad, and the ugly.
  • According to recent reports, the original Kindle Fire launched back when I was in high school, and despite 15 years of product name changes, frequent model refreshes, and an attempt to slowly move up-market, even Amazon’s bottom-of-the-barrel pricing couldn’t make up for missing apps and terrible performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I knew Amazon’s new flagship tablet was different when I found myself actually reaching for it.

Recent findings suggest that of course, you might be saying, that’s the job of a reviewer: to use the device throughout your daily life and let people know the good, the bad, and the ugly. But with the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro, I wasn’t just reaching for it when I thought a tablet might do the job. Over the past two weeks since receiving my review unit (the base nanomatte model), I’ve been pleasantly surprised by just how much I’ve preferred it over other devices. Hell, I’ve been reaching for Amazon’s slate over my Pixel 11 Pro XL, my MacBook Air, and even the pocket-friendly Lenovo Legion tablet I reviewed earlier this month, and considering this tech giant’s history with tablets, I’m as shocked as anyone.

According to recent reports, the original Kindle Fire launched back when I was in high school, and despite 15 years of product name changes, frequent model refreshes, and an attempt to slowly move up-market, even Amazon’s bottom-of-the-barrel pricing couldn’t make up for missing apps and terrible performance. But the Fire lineup is dead, replaced by a fresh lineup of more expensive “Alexa Tablets” that, nevertheless, remain a relative bargain in our ever-worsening gadget economy. This model, though, is a true iPad competitor. The Alexa Tablet 12 Pro attempts to correct every mistake Amazon has made with its tablet series over the past fifteen years, and somehow, for as low as $350 on sale, it basically pulls it all off.

Let’s get some of the most vital changes out of the way immediately before we get to the real star of the show. Most of Amazon’s specs sheet here won’t impress you, but context really means everything. A Mediatek Dimensity 8400 chipset paired with (in my test model) 8GB of RAM and 128GB of UFS 3.1 storage sounds like any run-of-the-mill midrange Android tablet. That’s a massive leap ahead of anything powering previous Fire Tablet models, though, and the option to move to a 256GB model with UFS 4.0 and 16GB of RAM does exist if you really feel like you need some extra power. This is also a completely unsubsidized tablet; regardless of which model you pick, you won’t have to pay $20 to remove lockscreen ads, something that remains an glitch on the cheaper Alexa Tablet 8 and 11 models.

Industry observers note that honestly, both the design and the overall feel of the hardware exceed my expectations; this is closer to Apple or Samsung’s premium tablet offerings than it is the Fire Tablets of yesteryear. It features an aluminum chassis with rounded edges and a thin, flat frame that — let’s be honest — looks right out of Apple’s typical iPad playbook. The power button doubles as a fingerprint sensor, while an indented groove below the volume buttons on the right side for its optional stylus. As someone who thinks this slate is better off for consumption than creation, it’s the one part of the design I question, though it also didn’t really bother me.

Without a doubt, the star of the show is this display. Amazon sent me the nanomatte version, available as a $50 upgrade over the $500 MSRP base model (the $650 256GB variant only comes in nanomatte). If you’re thinking of buying this tablet, the nanomatte model is without a doubt the one to spring for. It’s one of the nicer matte finishes I’ve seen on a device like this to date, and is absolutely the main reason I won’t stop reaching for this tablet. With a couple of tweaks — the saturation levels are a little too punchy out of the box for my liking, but Amazon’s “natural” color profile is a two-tap fix — this is as good as any non-OLED screen I can think of in recent memory. In fact, where Lenovo’s LCD panel had me wishing for next year’s rumored upgrade, I really never felt like OLED needed to be on Amazon’s flagship slate to make it worth my while.

No matter what I loaded up — The Odyssey, various episodes of TV or YouTube videos, the unofficial “Dusklight” port of Twilight Princess for Android — I just kept wanting to stare at this thing. I now totally understand why people spring for the nanomatte iPad Pro, and while I’m not trying to say this LCD holds a candle to one of the best OLED screens on the market right now, it’s nice to get this sort of finish on a tablet that doesn’t start at a whopping $1,800. (The iPad Pro itself starts at $1,200, but nanomatte is only available on 1TB or 2TB models, which I didn’t know until I sat down to write this review and is absolutely one of the dumbest things I’ve ever seen a organization of Apple’s size do. I digress.).

Amazon’s quad-stereo speakers sound excellent for a device of this size. They get surprisingly loud without much distortion, perfect for YouTube videos or streaming random movies, or even casual music listening. I’d still opt for headphones or external speakers for something you really care about (once again, The Odyssey being the perfect example), but that’s not exactly rare for a tablet. The fingerprint sensor is fast and mostly accurate, and the flashless 13MP rear-facing camera is… here, should you desperately need one. A more useful 8MP front-facing camera runs along the right side of the device, and there’s a single USB-C port at the bottom of the slate. No expandable storage options, something I’m genuinely disappointed about considering this slate tops out at just 256GB.

It has been revealed that of course, we have to address the Amazon-sized elephant in the room: the software. Unlike the “Fire OS” fork of Android that has resulted in years of Christmas morning Google searches to find out how to get YouTube on the tablet you just unwrapped, the Alexa Tablet is just… running Android. That includes some obvious quality-of-life improvements, like being able to transfer apps and other data directly from your phone or an older tablet, but yes, it also means the Play Store is here, along with practically every Android app you could hope for. Gmail, Chrome, Docs, Photos — everything’s here, and the ability to no longer have to hope that a good-enough replacement exists on the Amazon Appstore is such a relief. Hell, Amazon’s own app marketplace isn’t even pre-installed.

Now, with all of that noted, there are a couple of weird software quirks you should know going in. First, you’ll likely find a handful of applications unlisted from the Play Store as “unsupported” apps. This includes Amazon’s own software — the pre-loaded Amazon app is, bizarrely, just a web wrapper for the typical browser experience — and a smattering of random third-party applications, including the launcher Lawnchair, which I installed via the APK hosted on its website. That’s the second quirk: the default launcher is, as you might expect, themed around both Amazon and Alexa, complete with two unremovable widgets. It’s far from the worst home screen experience I’ve ever had, but a third-party launcher from the Play Store (or, again, from somewhere on the web) solves that problem. Save for the rare appearance of Amazon’s own dock and Alexa search bar when swiping back home, the third-party launcher experience here is great.

In a recent development, one more quick software positive: Amazon says it’ll support this tablet, along with the cheaper Alexa Tablet 11, through seven years of OS upgrades and security updates. We’ll have to see how frequent those updates arrive, but still — this experience feels built to last in a way Fire Tablets explicitly were not.

Recent findings suggest that the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro’s specs might not sound particularly impressive on paper, but I’ve had absolutely no performance complaints. Granted, I haven’t exactly pushed the envelope here — that Zelda shout-out is the most I’ve demanded graphically — but web pages loaded fast without crashes or reloads, apps stayed alive in the background, and moving around the OS generally felt snappy. If this bar sounds low, you probably never used a legacy Fire Tablet. Battery life, meanwhile, has been excellent, with a single charge typically getting me through a few days of mixed use. Charging speeds could be better, though, with a full charge taking nearly two hours to power the slate back up. That’s not enough reason to skip out on Amazon’s tablet, obviously, but it is one of those advantages that Samsung’s (much) more expensive Galaxy Tab S-series holds over it.

According to recent reports, it’s possible that my excitement over Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 12 Pro comes from a place of lowered expectations. I’m sure that’s true to some extent; again, 15 years of mostly-miserable experiences, up to and including the last time the company swung for a more premium slate, will do that to you. But considering Google’s disinterest in developing its own tablets and Samsung’s increasingly-ludicrous pricing for its higher-end options, I think this Alexa Tablet delivers a great alternative. Its specs are more than enough for the average Android user, and the things that I think people really care about on tablets — its display and its speakers — are among the best you can buy right now. Unless you really want to move into a four-figure price range for an OLED-equipped iPad or Galaxy Tab, I don’t really see a reason to shop around. And believe me, I’m still shocked.

Recent findings suggest that that’s especially true during Black Friday, which — despite this tablet launching just weeks prior — is deeply discounted for the holiday season. You can grab the base model Alexa Tablet 12 Pro for just $350, but you should spring for the nanomatte model at $400. That’s $150 off a price I already think isn’t terrible for the money, and frankly, an even stronger recommend if and when you can score it on sale.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson.
  • He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some upcoming tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand.
  • Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson. There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi. He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist.

He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some upcoming tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand. Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi's arm. He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with.

Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is not easy) and writing (also not easy).

What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself.

Sources indicate that he has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job. He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them. And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term.

Recent findings suggest that “While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”.

Industry observers note that the research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology. How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made?

According to recent reports, there may be some surprises along the way. Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist. Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out. What’s going on here? No one really knows.

In a recent development, scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either. Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains?

Recent findings suggest that avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year. After that? Again, no one knows. It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure. As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body.

I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted.

  • “Pass on our thanks to him, and also share the story of the Trump Corridor as well,” Ren told the Times.
  • Sources indicate that huawei executives call a gilded hallway at the headquarters the Trump Corridor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US sanctions pushed Huawei and China into self-reliance, and Huawei’s founder, Ren Zhengfei, wants Donald Trump thanked for it. Ren spoke to Keith Bradsher and Adam Satariano of The Fresh York Times at Huawei’s Shenzhen headquarters in October. The paper published the interview on Thursday.

“Pass on our thanks to him, and also share the story of the Trump Corridor as well,” Ren told the Times.

Sources indicate that huawei executives call a gilded hallway at the headquarters the Trump Corridor. It is named after the president whose first-term campaign tried to cut Huawei off from advanced chips and global telecoms networks. After the crackdown, Ren said, Huawei became “a company of our own country”. He is 82 and still Huawei’s chief executive.

In a recent development, the interview ran two days after a federal jury in Upcoming York convicted Huawei. The jury found it guilty of conspiring to steal trade secrets from US companies and of bank fraud linked to Iran. Huawei said the verdicts were “without legal or factual merit”.

It also came as the US tightened its curbs on Nvidia’s chips. On 16 November the US moved to restrict remote access to American AI chips through overseas data centres. Huawei’s Ascend processors have become China’s leading alternative to Nvidia’s chips, the Times reported.

Sources indicate that huawei now spends more than $27bn a year on research and development, according to the Times. It has worked with Chinese AI companies, including DeepSeek, to adapt their models to its chips. It argues it can rival Nvidia by linking many processors into one large system, even if each chip is weaker.

The gap remains wide. Huawei will make less than 4% as much AI computing power as Nvidia this year, research firm Epoch AI estimates. Its most powerful chip, the Ascend 950, delivers about half the performance of Nvidia’s H100, which began shipping in 2022.

In a recent development, china also still lacks the most advanced chipmaking equipment, including lithography machines from the Dutch organization ASML. Huawei has been working to fill other gaps at home, including its own AI memory.

Many in Trump’s first administration believed the restrictions could destroy Huawei, the Times reported.

“We thought this could be a death blow,” Liza Tobin, then a China policy official at the National Security Council, told the Times.

Sources indicate that ren, speaking before Nvidia’s recent leadership turmoil, said China would eventually overtake the US in chips. “It’s just a matter of time,” he said. He said he still hoped the two countries could repair their relationship.

“We have now established a complete chain that allows us to survive,” Ren told the Times.
